messages.content: You coach a learner of English (their own language is Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China)) who is rewriting part of a real post before publishing it. Two people talk to them: a reader from the community, who speaks English and reacts like a real person in the thread, and a tutor, who speaks English and addresses the learner informally, as a friendly tutor would. The writer may write to you in any language; whatever they write in, everything you write for them is in English.

Where it will be posted: the café's printed autumn menu. Readers: tourists who read English, choosing at the counter.
The writer's note about it, in their words: A translation of this source: 桂花拿铁：用店里自制的桂花糖浆调制，顶上撒一点海盐奶泡。
栗子巴斯克奶酪蛋糕：外表焦香，里面依然软嫩。
无酒精热红酒：加了肉桂、橙皮和丁香，适合阴雨天喝。
Given names and terms: Osmanthus latte, Basque cheesecake.
Title: Translate a café's new menu
The post so far:
<<<
Osmanthus latte: homemade osmanthus sauce, with a little sea salt milk cap.
Chestnut Basque cheesecake: the outside is baked golden-brown, the inside still soft.
Hot red wine (alcohol version): cinnamon, orange peel and clove, suitable for rainy days
>>>
The spot: "Chestnut Basque cheesecake: the outside is baked golden-brown, the inside still soft." in Chestnut Basque cheesecake: the outside is baked golden-brown, the inside still soft.
What is wrong there: Menu copy in English usually gives a short description of the result, such as a caramelised outside, rather than a full clause about how it was baked. The clause "the outside is baked golden-brown" still reads as a sentence about the kitchen, not a product description.
What the writer means (confirmed by them): 栗子巴斯克奶酪蛋糕：外表焦香，里面依然软嫩。
This is a translation of the source in the notes above: ref says exactly what the source says for this part, nothing it does not say (no added detail, image or emphasis). Where this text, as a fluent member of the community first wrote it, covers this part, it shows how they said it; take its wording unless the writer's own already works:
<<<
Osmanthus latte: house-made osmanthus syrup, a little sea-salt foam on top.
Chestnut basque cheesecake: caramelised outside, still soft inside.
Mulled wine (alcohol-free): cinnamon, orange peel and clove, for rainy days.
>>>
The learner will now write this part themselves in English. Prepare everything the session needs, in this order:
- reader: what the reader says on reaching this spot as it stands: one short line in English (at most 15 words), in character (puzzled, curious, teasing; never a teacher). The reader cannot read Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China): an untranslated passage is simply a gap to them, so react to what is missing and never mention the other language.
- replaces: exactly "Chestnut Basque cheesecake: the outside is baked golden-brown, the inside still soft.", copied character for character (the text around it is someone else's business). ref must fit in its place.
- keep: every point, detail, question, hedge and feeling in replaces, as short English notes, in order. The reference must carry each one unless the writer's meaning above drops it.
- ref: the reference version: what a fluent member of this community would write here to say exactly what the writer means, in the writer's voice and register. Keep everything the writer already says that still serves this meaning (their evidence, their reasoning, their own words) and add only what is missing. Never invent facts the writer has not given, here or in what they told you: no scene, event, line or detail from a work, no names, numbers, dates, quotes or personal circumstances. Where the meaning needs one (the evidence, which scene, what happened to them), write a short placeholder in its place, in English, between ⟨ and ⟩ (for example ⟨the scene you mean⟩), and the writer will fill it in. Where the problem is how the sentence is built (order, emphasis, angle, nominalisation), rebuild it the way this community would say it; do not stop at the smallest fix. Keep the strength the writer confirmed: where the problem is how something lands on its reader (too pushy, too blunt) and the writer means a firm need, a request or a demand, say it the way this place says such things politely and keep it firm; never turn it into something optional or a passing wish. Where the writer reached for an image or a joke, use this community's own equivalent if it has one rather than flattening it into plain words. Where the writer built a figure on purpose (a parallel or echo, a deliberate repetition, wordplay), ref keeps the figure and only puts natural words into it; the why note for such a word says the figure works and why the word changes. ref never says again what the post already says right before or after the replaced text (a reason or detail the next sentence gives stays there). ref replaces exactly the replaces text and carries every keep note and every name, title or label in it (a dish's name before its description, a person's name); it is the final text for that span: anything else wrong or unnatural inside it is fixed too, even where it is the writer's own wording. The writer's voice stays: casual spelling and capitalisation (all lowercase, capitals for emphasis, keysmashes, stretched letters, a missing apostrophe in a contraction), slang, emoji and the community's own shorthand, wherever fluent members of this community write that way too; so does a greeting or a word from another language used as flavour that readers will get. Names (characters, people, usernames, places, the community's terms) are the writer's: leave how they spell and capitalise them and which name they use, unless a reader could not tell who is meant. None of these is a problem in either pass. But wording carried over from Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China) (a calque, a collocation, structure or set phrase a fluent writer would not produce) is not voice: it is a problem however casual the post. ref keeps that voice. Put [square brackets] around two to four single words that carry the key choices.
- alts: one or two other natural ways to say it, without brackets.
- pieces: three to eight hint pieces: the content words and short collocations (one to three words) that carry the meaning, including the writer's own words worth reusing. Each piece is English words only: no grammar notes, glosses, symbols or instructions. A piece names a word, never how to use it ("worth", not "worth + -ing" or "worth coming"). Not consecutive chunks of ref, no function-word glue, no full clauses: the learner must still build the sentence. "x / y" offers a fork.
- construct: the one reusable pattern this spot teaches, as a learner would jot it in a notebook: at most eight words, a English frame with one placeholder ("X left him + adjective", "What really got me was …"), optionally a short English gloss. Not a grammar formula.
- why: one entry per choice in ref that the learner might not make themselves. label: the English words; note, in English: why this choice here, contrasted with what the learner wrote or would likely write, with a nuance or a tiny example when it helps. Concrete and specific, never "more natural" or "more appropriate" alone.
- checks: the mistakes this learner is likely to make on a first try, most important first: missing a part of the meaning, a structure carried over from Simplified Chinese (as used in mainland China), the specific error already in their draft, a wrong word for this sense. For each: problem (what the grader should look for, in English); reader (optional: how the reader reacts when it happens, one English line in character, only when the meaning really suffers); hint (English: a nudge that points at the gap without giving the words); tell (English: says the fix plainly, with the words).
- success: the reader's reaction once the learner gets it right: in English, in character, at most 12 words, a reaction to what is now said (not a summary of it).
- prompt: the tutor's instruction in English to start writing: one short sentence that fits the size of the spot (a clause, a sentence, a passage). The writer has just confirmed what they mean, so do not restate it; never mention punctuation, span boundaries or what comes after; never contain any word or structure from ref.

Is the middle actually soft, or dry?","replaces":"Chestnut Basque cheesecake: the outside is baked golden-brown, the inside still soft.","keep":["Chestnut Basque cheesecake: the name and its label come first, before the description.","The outside is the focus: the browned, appetising surface of the cake.","Golden-brown: the colour of the outside.","Still soft: the inside stays soft even though the outside is browned (依然).","Soft and tender: the inside's texture is soft and tender, not just soft (软嫩)."],"ref":"Chestnut Basque cheesecake: golden-brown, [caramelised] outside, [still] soft and [tender] inside.","alts":["Chestnut Basque cheesecake: toasty, browned outside, still soft and tender inside.","Chestnut Basque cheesecake: browned and toasty on the outside, soft and tender in the middle."],"pieces":["caramelised","tender","browned","toasty","soft middle"],"construct":"Dish name: [adjective] outside, [adjective] inside","why":[{"label":"golden-brown","note":"Keeps the writer's colour point but as an adjective describing the cake. \"Baked golden-brown\" is a sentence about the kitchen; a menu describes what the customer will see."},{"label":"caramelised","note":"A menu term for the browned, slightly sweet crust. It suggests 焦香 without the negative sense of \"burnt\" or \"scorched\", which would put readers off."},{"label":"still","note":"The writer's 依然 sets up a contrast: the outside is browned, yet the inside is still soft. Without \"still\", the sentence just lists two qualities and loses that point."},{"label":"tender","note":"Covers 嫩 as well as 软. \"Soft\" alone can sound like dry or undercooked; \"soft and tender\" tells the customer the texture is pleasant."}],"checks":[{"problem":"The sentence describes the baking process (baked, oven, time) instead of what the cake looks and feels like.","reader":"Baked how long? I just want to know if it's good!","hint":"Think about what the customer sees on the plate, not what happened in the oven.","tell":"Describe the result, not the process: write \"golden-brown\" as an adjective and drop \"baked\"."},{"problem":"The contrast from 依然 is lost: the inside is described as soft without \"still\", so it reads as a separate fact rather than something that survives the browning.","reader":null,"hint":"The word should show that the soft texture carries on despite the browned outside.","tell":"Add \"still\" before \"soft\" in the inside clause."},{"problem":"Translation of 焦香 as \"burnt\", \"scorched\" or \"charred\", which sounds like a mistake rather than an appetising finish.","reader":"Burnt? Hmm, I'm not sure I want that one.","hint":"You want a word that makes the crust sound good, like something a café would say proudly.","tell":"Use \"caramelised\" or \"toasty\" for the outside."},{"problem":"The texture is reduced to plain \"soft\" (missing 嫩), which can sound dry or undercooked.","reader":null,"hint":"Think about how the middle feels to eat, and add a second word that makes it sound pleasant.","tell":"Use \"soft and tender\" for the inside."},{"problem":"The colour point (golden-brown) is dropped, leaving the outside with no description.","reader":null,"hint":"The outside needs more than a flavour word; say how it looks as well.","tell":"Keep \"golden-brown\" as an adjective before the outside, alongside the other word for the surface."}],"success":"Oh, that sounds lovely. I'll order that one.","prompt":"Now describe this cake for the menu, starting with the crust and then the middle."}
